corrected_value.title: The Impact of Resource Scarcity on Price-Quality Judgments
corrected_value.title_o: The Impact of Resource Scarcity on Price-Quality Judgments

decisions.quote: In this sixth installment of Data Replicada, we report our attempt to replicate a recently published Journal of Consumer Research (JCR) article entitled, “The Impact of Resource Scarcity on Price-Quality Judgments” ( .html ). This one was full of surprises. The primary thesis of this article is straightforward: “Scarcity decreases consumers’ tendency to use price to judge product quality.” It reports six studies, three of which were conducted on MTurk. We chose to replicate Study 2A (N = 149) because it was the MTurk study with the strongest evidence, and because it also tested the effects of scarcity on two other measures: desire for abundance and categorization tendency (described below).
decisions.reason: The primary report explicitly identifies the replicated original study as the recently published Journal of Consumer Research article entitled 'The Impact of Resource Scarcity on Price-Quality Judgments' (specifically replicating Study 2A). Both the shipped row (input_row_index 2714) and blind coding (target_index 0) identify this exact article; the blind coding left author, year, and DOI fields blank only because the extracted blog post text replaced the hyperlink with '( .html )' and lacked a reference list. Other works mentioned in the post (Roux, Goldsmith, and Bonezzi 2015 for the borrowed scarcity writing prompt; Booth 1984 and Lynn 1991 in author feedback) are manipulation-source or background citations rather than replicated targets.

decisions.quote: On the one hand, we were successful at dramatically reducing attrition. On the other hand, we were unsuccessful at reducing differential attrition, as once again many more participants dropped out of the Scarcity condition than the Control condition. So then we gave up, and decided to call the whole thing “inconclusive.”
decisions.reason: Although the initial replication attempt produced statistically significant effects on price-quality correlation and categorization tendency (which the authors initially note 'looks like at least a partial success'), the authors demonstrate that severe differential attrition compromised random assignment and yielded a disproportionate share of 'Bad Responders' in the Scarcity condition, invalidating between-condition comparisons ('differential attrition means that we cannot validly compare Good Responders in the Control condition to Good Responders in the Scarcity condition... the jury is still out because a true test of this hypothesis would require conducting a study that eliminates the problem of differential attrition'). After a pre-registered follow-up study (N = 2,101) also failed to eliminate differential attrition, the authors state their overall verdict on the replication effort: 'So then we gave up, and decided to call the whole thing “inconclusive.”' Under the codebook, when the authors' own overall verdict is that a methodological defect (differential attrition compromising random assignment) prevents their attempt from providing a valid, meaningful test of the original hypothesis, the outcome is 'uninformative', not 'mixed'.

decisions.quote: In this sixth installment of Data Replicada, we report our attempt to replicate a recently published Journal of Consumer Research (JCR) article entitled, “The Impact of Resource Scarcity on Price-Quality Judgments” ( .html ).
decisions.reason: Both shipped and blind codings agree that the record is a 'replication'. The authors collected new data across multiple independent MTurk samples to re-test the findings of Study 2A of the original JCR article (while the re-analysis of original data mentioned at the end of the post is merely commentary contributed by the original authors in the 'Author feedback' section).
